title: After the fall
hookLine: despair, and slowly new movements of piety and learning

cards: Back in Hamburg, the barrels are still standing in Glückel's house: linen, peas, dried meat, packed for a journey that is not going to happen.
In her telling, they waited a long while, and in the end they were opened and the food used up. It's a small, almost ordinary scene. Someone has to decide when to unpack.
Someone has to cook the beans meant for the road. That moment, multiplied across a whole people, is today's story.

teach.b: When news of the conversion spread, shame and grief came first. People had sold homes, fasted, announced the end of exile, and now had to face their neighbors.
Some followers kept believing in secret, which kept rabbis wary long afterward.
Teachers grew suspicious of anyone claiming special revelation, and some communities limited the study of mystical texts to older, learned students. The rabbis also had an old warning.
The Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, speaks harshly of those who calculate the end, because when the date passes, people lose hope altogether. The point was not to stop hoping.
It was to stop setting dates. Then, slowly, something grew in the space the disappointment left: not a new announcement, but a turn inward, toward steady work.
An Italian kabbalist, Moshe Chaim Luzzatto, wrote a book called The Path of the Upright.

teach.h: A LADDER, ONE RUNG AT A TIME.
teach.b: It takes an old rabbinic teaching, a ladder of qualities that starts with watchfulness and zeal and climbs toward holiness, and walks up it one rung at a time, with plain advice for ordinary days.
In Eastern Europe, new circles of prayer and learning were forming, and one of them would soon change Jewish life.
The Psalms had already spoken to this kind of night: "Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy cometh in the morning."
After the fall there was no single morning, but a slow dawn, built by people who unpacked their barrels and kept going.

how: Luzzatto's The Path of the Upright is still studied in yeshivas and study groups, often slowly, a chapter at a time, as a guide to character.

games.q: you are a teacher in a community that believed and was let down. a new man arrives claiming special revelation. what do you do?
o: be wary, and keep teaching steady, ordinary practice.
games.why: after the fall, rabbis grew wary of such claims, and new teachers turned to slow, step-by-step piety and learning.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that didn't happen the way you hoped, not the biggest, something you can hold, and notice what you packed for it: plans, money, words already said.

Ask which one barrel you could unpack, one plan to let go of or one thing to put to ordinary use; you don't have to feel fine about it. If you pray, you can bring the disappointment with you in your own words.
